summary:
National police are the documented source of the most serious risk. In September 2017 officers in Baku detained at least 100 people in raids presented as action against prostitution. Detainees were beaten, interrogated, subjected to forced medical examinations and blackmailed, and a United States State Department report covering that period recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 of those held were imprisoned or fined, and the detentions formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games. Human Rights Watch called for an investigation and for releases. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and the mistreatment.

Operations of this kind continued. In July 2023 officers raided a private birthday party in Baku, where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing. That raid is the most recent police action against LGBT people documented in the sources available here; no later instance is sourced.

A trans woman was murdered in Baku in March 2024 and the police investigation was inadequate, in the finding of ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025. No later killing of a trans person in Azerbaijan is documented in these sources.

Identity documents are a fixed obstacle. Transgender people cannot change their gender on official documents, though they may change their name to match their gender identity. A shadow report submitted to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women by the Gender and Development Social Union states that changing identity documents is impossible for trans women.

Legal protection is close to absent. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned. Marriage and civil unions are neither recognised nor performed for couples classed locally as same-sex, and such couples may not adopt children. The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex.

Hostility from state-linked media is documented. In 2024 the state-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march in Baku demanding access to trans healthcare. Politicians and officials have used discriminatory language to shape public perception, and the 2017 US State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and blocking of websites.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49 of 49, in its European review every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection. The ranking is an index position rather than a measure of incident rates, but it places the country at the bottom of the comparison set for the whole period.

QueeRadar monitoring found that 77% of 428 media pieces analysed in 2023 were hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people. In the same year an activist in Baku was told to remove a rainbow flag from a cafe, an instance of ordinary-space pressure that sits alongside the documented police action.

Accountability for the September 2017 raids arrived through an international court rather than a domestic one: Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019 and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in April 2024. The sources document no domestic criminal proceeding against the officers involved.
localsOnly:
Conscription is a documented route to forced disclosure. Able-bodied men aged 18 to 35 are subject to military service, and under the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Article 18/b (personality disorders) and Article 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders). Queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing.

Discrimination has direct economic effects on residents. Trans people are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. OC Media profiles 'Durdana', 29, who was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

A shadow report to the CEDAW committee by the Gender and Development Social Union documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia and transphobia in official and private media, and forced marriages; the organisation reports serving more than 200 LBT people. The same review period records a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out.

In April 2019 Elina Hajiyeva, 14, of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school. The principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance; she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) in compensation. The case prompted a nationwide social media campaign and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019, with a new hotline to improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.

Resident-facing support infrastructure exists despite the legal position. The Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), established 2020, is a queer-feminist platform created in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face.

LGBTQIA+ media operates openly: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011, and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, was founded in December 2015 and became an NGO in August 2017. A documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support, drawing about 80 people.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2024 murder investigation has since progressed is not sourced here, and no domestic proceeding arising from it is documented.

By law no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS, but it is unknown whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate.

The constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct; whether it has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics is not known.

Every incident documented in these sources takes place in Baku. Practice in other cities is not described, and the absence of later raids after July 2023 reflects the limits of the sources rather than a finding about current enforcement.
